cells.value: Agents × UPI: what machine payments can learn from UPI
cells.text: Agents × UPI: what machine payments can learn from UPI

cells.value: Deon Menezes, Piyush Maheshwari, Naina Sachdev
cells.text: Deon Menezes, Piyush Maheshwari, Naina Sachdev

cells.value: UPI did not win by being the smartest payment technology. It won because India treated the rail as shared, open public infrastructure and let apps compete on top. Agents now pay for services, pay each other and spend on behalf of people, with no human confirming each step. What should machine payments copy from UPI? Vishnu traces the shared history and principles behind UPI, blockchains and agentic payments, and how UPI reached mass adoption. Piyush covers how authority gets granted: shared rails, interoperability by default, scoped delegation, and mandates that can be changed or revoked in real time. Naina covers what happens after the agent spends: once the PIN is gone, how do we prove a payment matched its mandate, settle disputes, produce receipts that reconcile, and keep payments private but auditable?

cells.value: Glamsterdam raises Ethereum's gas limit from 60M to 200M and reprices EVM operations, so every gas cost has to match how long clients actually take to execute it. cells.value: In optimistic governance, a proposal passes by default unless holders object within a set window. The holder’s right shifts from voting yes or no to blocking what they disagree with. That lowers the turnout problem, but it raises new questions: who is watching when nobody votes, how high should the veto bar be, and what stops a team from passing things quietly? This session covers how the model works, where it is already in use, and what holders give up and gain when silence counts as consent.

cells.value:
Private companies, especially fintechs, handle large volumes of small-value customer complaints. Doing this through internal support or the courts is often slow, expensive and seen as biased in the company’s favour. This session looks at Lemon, an Argentine crypto app that sends some consumer complaints to an independent, crowdsourced juror panel. 
​
​We’ll cover:
- What kinds of disputes it’s used for and how the process works from start to finish
- How it fits alongside consumer protection law and existing complaint channels
- What it changes for user trust and for the company’s costs
- Its limits and open questions, such as enforceability, juror incentives and which cases shouldn’t go this route


It’s useful for anyone in fintech, compliance or legal ops who is weighing alternatives to traditional complaint handling.
